title: The Four Forms: A, E, I, O
short: A: All S are P. E: No S are P. I: Some S are P. O: Some S are not P. Quantity is universal or particular; quality is affirmative or negative.
trouble: Reading "some" as "some but not all": in logic, "Some S are P" means at least one, and it stays true even if all S are P.

blocks.html: There are exactly four ways to relate two classes in a categorical proposition. Medieval logicians named them with the vowels of AffIrmo ("I affirm") and nEgO ("I deny").

blocks.cap: S is the subject term, P the predicate term.

blocks.html: Quantity asks "all or some?": A and E are universal, I and O particular. Quality asks "including or excluding?": A and I are affirmative, E and O negative. In logic, some means "at least one".

"Some" means at least one because logic only keeps what a statement guarantees. "Some students passed" guarantees that at least one did. It does not guarantee that some failed; the speaker may simply not know. If all of them passed, "Some students passed" is still true, just not the whole story.

blocks.title: When all of them are
blocks.q: Every student in the class passed the quiz. Is "Some students in the class are students who passed" true?
steps: In logic, "some" asks only for at least one.
There is at least one student in the class, and that student passed.
So the I statement is true, even though the A statement is true as well.

blocks.html: Reading "some" as "some but not all". If every S is P (and there are S), then "Some S are P" is true. Check: ask whether the statement would become false if it turned out that all of them are. For "some", it would not.
